p.facts: Under CPG, the spouses used conjugal funds to build a P4 million house on the husband's exclusive lot, worth P800,000 at the time. The house increased the property's value. At liquidation, the husband claims the house and lot as his.
p.q: Who owns the house and lot?
alac: The entire property becomes conjugal, upon reimbursement to the husband of the lot's value.

The law provides that when the cost of the improvement made with conjugal funds and any resulting increase in value are more than the value of the exclusive property at the time of the improvement, the entire property shall belong to the conjugal partnership, subject to reimbursement of the value of the property to the owner-spouse, ownership vesting at the time of the liquidation.
Here, the P4 million house and the increase in value exceed the P800,000 lot.
Therefore, the house and lot become conjugal upon reimbursement of P800,000 to the husband.
p.key: TWIST: “owned before marriage” loses when the conjugal improvement is worth more. Ownership vests upon reimbursement at liquidation.

P.title: Debts for the family's benefit
P.rule: The conjugal partnership answers for debts that benefited the family; benefit is presumed when a spouse borrows for his own business, but must be proved when he acts as surety for another.

p.label: Surety for a friend's company
p.facts: Under CPG, Wil signed as surety for a P10 million loan of his friend's corporation, in which Wil had no shares. The corporation defaulted and the bank levied on the conjugal house.
p.q: Is the conjugal partnership liable?
p.hint: Is benefit to the family presumed for a surety?
alac: No. The conjugal partnership is not liable.

The law provides that the conjugal partnership is liable for debts contracted by a spouse to the extent the family benefited. Jurisprudence provides that when a spouse acts as surety for another, benefit to the family is not presumed and must be proved; incidental benefits are not enough.
Here, Wil signed as surety for a company in which he had no shares. No benefit to his family was shown.
Therefore, the conjugal house cannot be levied on for this debt.
p.key: Surety → prove the benefit (Ayala Investment).

p.label: Officer-shareholder signs as surety
p.facts: Same facts, but Wil was a minor shareholder and officer, and the bank shows only that the loan helped keep his job and might raise the value of his shares.
p.q: Is the conjugal partnership liable?
alac: No. The conjugal partnership is still not liable.

Jurisprudence provides that when a spouse acts as surety for a corporation, benefits such as continued employment or a possible rise in the value of shares are merely incidental and do not prove benefit to the family.
Here, the bank showed only that the loan kept Wil employed and might raise his share value. These are incidental benefits.
Therefore, the conjugal partnership is not liable.
p.key: Incidental benefits do not count; the benefit must be direct and actual.

p.label: Loan for his own clinic
p.facts: Under CPG, Dr. Xavi borrowed P2 million in his own name to equip his medical clinic, the family's main income source. The loan is unpaid.
p.q: Is the conjugal partnership liable?
alac: Yes. The conjugal partnership is liable.
Jurisprudence provides that when a spouse contracts a loan for his own business or profession, it is presumed to redound to the benefit of the family, and the conjugal partnership is liable.
Here, Dr. Xavi borrowed the money in his own name to equip his own clinic, which supports the family.
Therefore, the conjugal partnership is liable for the loan.
p.key: TWIST: borrower for his OWN business or profession → benefit presumed.

P.title: Judicial separation of property
P.rule: During the marriage, separation of property happens only by judicial order, on the grounds in Art. 135 or by voluntary joint petition.

p.label: Separated for two years
p.facts: Yolly and Zandro have lived apart for two years. Zandro lives with another woman, and they have not spoken since. Yolly wants to protect her earnings.
p.q: May Yolly obtain judicial separation of property?
alac: Yes. Yolly may obtain judicial separation of property.

The law provides that a spouse may petition for judicial separation of property when, at the time of the petition, the spouses have been separated in fact for at least one year and reconciliation is highly improbable.
Here, they have been separated for two years, Zandro lives with another woman, and they no longer communicate.
Therefore, Yolly may obtain judicial separation of property.
p.key: Two requirements: at least 1 year AND reconciliation highly improbable.

p.label: Husband convicted with civil interdiction
p.facts: Anton was sentenced by final judgment to reclusion temporal, which carries civil interdiction. His wife Bella files a petition for judicial separation of property and attaches the judgment.
p.q: Is the final judgment enough to grant the petition?
p.hint: Some grounds are proved by the judgment alone.
alac: Yes. The final judgment is enough.

The law provides that a spouse may petition for judicial separation of property when the other has been sentenced to a penalty carrying civil interdiction, and that the final judgment is enough basis for the grant.
Here, Anton was sentenced by final judgment to a penalty carrying civil interdiction.
Therefore, the court may grant the petition on the basis of the judgment.
p.key: For civil interdiction, absence, and loss of parental authority, the final judgment is enough.

p.label: Short trip and a quarrel
p.facts: After a quarrel, Carlo moved to his mother's house for two months but still sends money and calls the children daily. His wife Dina petitions for judicial separation of property on the ground of abandonment.
p.q: Will the petition prosper?
alac: No. The petition will not prosper.

The law provides that a spouse is deemed to have abandoned the other when he has left the conjugal dwelling without intention of returning, which is presumed only after three months without news of his whereabouts; separation in fact must also last at least one year to be a ground.
Here, Carlo left only two months ago, still supports the family, and keeps in touch daily. There is no abandonment and no separation in fact for one year.
Therefore, no ground for judicial separation of property exists.
p.key: TWIST: leaving the house ≠ abandonment. Check the 3-month presumption and the 1-year rule.

P.title: Article 147 vs. Article 148
P.rule: Art. 147 (capacitated, exclusive cohabitation) presumes joint efforts and equal shares, and counts homemaking; Art. 148 (all others) requires proof of actual contribution and shares in proportion.

p.label: Homemaker partner
p.facts: Ely and Faye, both single and free to marry each other, lived together for 12 years. Faye kept house and raised their children; Ely bought a house and lot with his salary, titled in his name. They separated.
p.q: How is the house and lot divided?
p.hint: Which article applies, and does homemaking count?
alac: It is owned by Ely and Faye in equal shares.

The law provides that when a man and a woman capacitated to marry each other live exclusively together as husband and wife without marriage, property acquired while they lived together is presumed obtained by their joint efforts and owned in equal shares, and a party who cared for the family and household is deemed to have contributed.
Here, Ely and Faye were both free to marry each other and lived together exclusively. The house was acquired during their cohabitation, and Faye's homemaking counts as contribution.
Therefore, they own the house and lot in equal shares.
p.key: Art. 147: equal shares + homemaking counts, regardless of whose name is on the title.

p.label: Void marriage under Art. 36
p.facts: Gil and Hana's marriage was declared void for psychological incapacity. During the marriage, they bought a condominium with their salaries. Gil argues the rules on CPG liquidation apply.
p.q: What governs their property?
alac: Article 147 governs, and the condominium is liquidated under the rules on co-ownership.

Jurisprudence provides that when a marriage is void for psychological incapacity and the parties were capacitated to marry each other, their property relations are governed by the special co-ownership of parties who live together without a valid marriage, and are liquidated under the rules on co-ownership.
Here, the marriage was void for psychological incapacity, and both were capacitated to marry each other.
Therefore, the condominium is co-owned in equal shares under Article 147.
p.key: Valdes v. RTC: Art. 36 void marriage → Art. 147, not ACP or CPG.

p.label: Married man's mistress
p.facts: Ivo, married to Jen, lived with Kat. A house was bought during Ivo and Kat's cohabitation, titled in Kat's name. Kat proved she paid the entire price from her business; Ivo offered no proof of contribution but claims half.
p.q: Does Ivo own half the house?
p.hint: Which article applies when one party is married?
alac: No. The house belongs to Kat alone.

The law provides that in cohabitation not falling under the rules for capacitated parties, only property acquired through actual joint contribution of money, property, or industry is owned in common, in proportion to contributions. Jurisprudence requires proof of actual contribution.
Here, Ivo was married to Jen, so Article 148 applies. Kat proved she paid the full price, and Ivo proved no contribution.
Therefore, Kat owns the house alone.
p.key: TWIST: one party married → Art. 148 → no presumption of joint effort (Atienza v. De Castro).

P.title: Earnest efforts in suits between family members
P.rule: A suit between members of the same family must show in a verified pleading that earnest efforts toward a compromise were made and failed, unless a non-family member is a party or the matter cannot be compromised.

p.label: Siblings fighting over land
p.facts: Lara sued her brother Migs to recover a lot. Her verified complaint did not allege any efforts to settle. Migs moved to dismiss.
p.q: Should the complaint be dismissed?
alac: Yes. The complaint should be dismissed.

The law provides that no suit between members of the same family shall prosper unless the verified complaint shows that earnest efforts toward a compromise have been made but failed. Family relations include those among brothers and sisters.
Here, Lara and Migs are siblings, and her complaint does not show any earnest efforts toward a compromise.
Therefore, the complaint should be dismissed.
p.key: Family = spouses, parents and children, ascendants and descendants, siblings.

p.label: Efforts made but failed
p.facts: Before suing her father for her share in the rentals of their co-owned building, Nora asked him twice in writing to meet, and they met once at the barangay hall, but he refused any settlement. Her verified complaint alleges these facts.
p.q: Has Nora complied with the requirement?
alac: Yes. Nora has complied.

The law provides that the verified complaint must show that earnest efforts toward a compromise were made but failed. Jurisprudence provides that the law requires genuine efforts, not a successful settlement.
Here, Nora made written requests and met with her father at the barangay hall, and he refused to settle. Her verified complaint alleges these facts.
Therefore, the requirement is satisfied.
p.key: Show BOTH the attempt and its failure.

p.label: Suing a sister-in-law
p.facts: Olga sued her brother and his wife for damages over a boundary dispute. The complaint does not allege earnest efforts toward a compromise.
p.q: Must the complaint be dismissed?
alac: No. The complaint should not be dismissed on this ground.

The law provides that the earnest-efforts requirement applies to suits between members of the same family. Jurisprudence provides that the enumeration is exclusive and does not include in-laws, so the requirement does not apply when a non-family member is a party.
Here, Olga's sister-in-law is a co-defendant. She is not a family member under the law.
Therefore, the requirement does not apply, and the complaint should not be dismissed.
p.key: TWIST: one in-law as a party takes the case out of Art. 151 (Hontiveros; Gayon).

P.title: Family home exemption
P.rule: The family home is exempt from execution except for taxes, debts before constitution, mortgage debts, and debts for its construction; the exemption does not cover debts incurred before the Family Code took effect.

p.label: Credit-card judgment
p.facts: Pia and Quin have lived in their house and lot since 2010. In 2023, Quin incurred a P300,000 credit-card debt. The bank obtained a judgment and levied on the house, worth P250,000 when it became the family home.
p.q: Can the house be sold to satisfy the judgment?
p.hint: Is a credit-card debt among the exceptions?
alac: No. The house is exempt from execution.

The law provides that the family home is exempt from execution, forced sale, or attachment, except for nonpayment of taxes, debts incurred before its constitution, debts secured by mortgages on it, and debts due to those who built it, and up to the value allowed by law.

Here, the house became the family home in 2010, and the credit-card debt was incurred in 2023, after constitution. It is not a tax, mortgage, or construction debt, and the home's value is within the limit.
Therefore, the house cannot be sold to satisfy the judgment.
p.key: Debt AFTER constitution, not among the four exceptions → exempt.

p.label: Unpaid builders
p.facts: Rino built his house in 2024 and moved in with his family. He never paid the contractor and the hardware supplier. They obtained judgments and levied on the house.
p.q: Is the house exempt?
alac: No. The house is not exempt.

The law provides that the family home is not exempt from execution for debts due to laborers, mechanics, architects, builders, materialmen, and others who rendered service or furnished materials for its construction.
Here, the creditors are the contractor and supplier who built and supplied the materials for the house.
Therefore, the house may be levied on to pay them.
p.key: It would be unjust to enjoy a house while refusing to pay those who built it.

p.label: Debt before the Family Code
p.facts: Sol has lived in his house since 1980. In 1986, he incurred a debt that ended in a judgment against him. In 2026, the creditor levies on the house. Sol claims the family-home exemption.
p.q: Is the house exempt?
alac: No. The house is not exempt from this debt.

The law provides that existing family residences are deemed family homes under the Family Code. Jurisprudence provides that the exemption does not apply to debts incurred before the Family Code took effect on August 3, 1988.
Here, the debt was incurred in 1986, before the Family Code took effect.
Therefore, the house may be levied on for this debt.
p.key: TWIST: Modequillo. The family home status is retroactive; the exemption is not.

P.title: Family home after the head of the family dies
P.rule: The family home continues for 10 years from the death, or as long as there is a minor beneficiary, and the heirs cannot partition it unless the court finds compelling reasons.

p.label: Partition after 3 years
p.facts: Tito died in 2023, survived by his wife and three adult children, all living in the family home. In 2026, one child asks the court to partition the house.
p.q: May the house be partitioned?
p.hint: How long does the family home continue?
alac: No. The house may not be partitioned yet, unless the court finds compelling reasons.

The law provides that the family home shall continue despite the death of one or both spouses for a period of ten years or for as long as there is a minor beneficiary, and the heirs cannot partition it during that period unless the court finds compelling reasons.
Here, Tito died in 2023, so only three years have passed.
Therefore, partition is not allowed unless the court finds compelling reasons.
p.key: 10 years OR a minor beneficiary, whichever is longer.

p.label: Minor beneficiary after 12 years
p.facts: Uro died in 2013. His 14-year-old son, whom Uro supported until his death and who is now supported by his mother, the widow, still lives in the family home. In 2026, the adult children ask for partition.
p.q: May the house be partitioned?
p.hint: Is there still a minor beneficiary?
alac: No. The house may not be partitioned.

The law provides that the family home continues for ten years or for as long as there is a minor beneficiary. A beneficiary is a relative who lives in the family home and depends on the head of the family for legal support.
Here, more than 10 years have passed, but Uro's 14-year-old son is a minor child of the head of family, lives in the house, and depended on him for support.
Therefore, the house remains a family home while he is a minor.
p.key: The minor beneficiary extends protection beyond 10 years.

p.label: Grandson supported by his own father
p.facts: Vida's husband died in 2010. In 2026, Vida and one son seek partition. The other son objects because his own minor son lives in the house. The grandson is supported by his own father, not by the deceased.
p.q: May the family home be partitioned?
alac: Yes. The family home may be partitioned.

The law provides that the family home continues for ten years from death or while there is a minor beneficiary. Jurisprudence provides that a beneficiary must live in the family home and depend on the head of the family for legal support.
Here, more than 10 years have passed. The grandson lives in the house but depends on his own father for support, not on the head of the family, so he is not a beneficiary.
Therefore, the family home may be partitioned.
p.key: TWIST: Patricio v. Dario. Living in the house is not enough; dependence on the head is required.

P.title: Impugning legitimacy
P.rule: A child conceived or born during a valid marriage is legitimate; only the husband (or his heirs in limited cases) may impugn it, on the Art. 166 grounds, within 1, 2, or 3 years.

p.label: Husband in prison
p.facts: Will was in prison with no conjugal visits for the whole year before his wife Xyla gave birth. He lives in Manila; the child was born and registered in Manila. He learned of the birth on the same day.
p.q: May Will impugn the child's legitimacy, and within what period?
alac: Yes, within one year from his knowledge of the birth.

The law provides that legitimacy may be impugned on the ground of physical impossibility of sexual intercourse within the first 120 days of the 300 days before the birth, such as when the spouses live separately so that intercourse is not possible. The action must be brought within one year from knowledge of the birth if the husband resides in the place of birth or its recording.
Here, Will was in prison without conjugal visits for the entire period. He lives in Manila, where the child was born and registered.
Therefore, Will may impugn the child's legitimacy within one year from learning of the birth.
p.key: Same city or municipality = 1 year; elsewhere in the Philippines = 2; abroad = 3.

p.label: Mother names another man
p.facts: Yna, married to Zed, gave birth while still living with him. She filed the birth certificate naming her lover, Abe, as the father.
p.q: Whose child is the baby in law?
p.hint: Can the mother's declaration defeat legitimacy?
alac: The baby is the legitimate child of Yna and Zed.
The law provides that children conceived or born during the marriage are legitimate, and that a child shall be considered legitimate although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy.
Here, the baby was born during the marriage of Yna and Zed. Yna's naming of Abe as father is only her declaration.
Therefore, the baby is legitimate, unless Zed impugns legitimacy in a proper action.
p.key: The mother cannot impugn; only the husband can.

p.label: Biological father sues
p.facts: Bert claims he is the biological father of a child born to Cora during her subsisting marriage to Dan. Dan has never questioned the child's legitimacy. Bert files a petition to have the child recognized as his illegitimate child.
p.q: Will Bert's petition prosper?
alac: No. Bert's petition will not prosper.

The law provides that a child born during a valid marriage is presumed legitimate. Jurisprudence provides that only the husband, or his heirs in the cases allowed by law, may impugn legitimacy, and legitimacy cannot be attacked collaterally; the child, however, keeps her own right to establish her biological filiation.
Here, the child was born during Cora and Dan's marriage, and Dan never impugned the child's legitimacy. Bert is not a proper party.
Therefore, his petition cannot prosper.
p.key: TWIST: the biological father has no standing (Liyao; Cua Ko). Note the child's own separate right.

P.title: Proof and actions for filiation
P.rule: Filiation is proved by primary evidence (birth record, final judgment, signed admission) or, if absent, secondary evidence; an illegitimate child relying on secondary evidence must sue during the alleged parent's lifetime.

p.label: Signed letter
p.facts: Eli, an illegitimate child, sues his alleged father Fred for support. Eli presents a handwritten letter signed by Fred saying, “I am proud to be your father.”
p.q: Is Eli's filiation proved?
alac: Yes. Eli's filiation is proved.

The law provides that filiation of illegitimate children is established in the same way as legitimate filiation, including an admission of filiation in a private handwritten instrument signed by the parent concerned, which is primary evidence.
Here, Fred wrote and signed a letter admitting he is Eli's father.
Therefore, Eli's filiation is established, and he may claim support.
p.key: Signed handwritten admission = primary evidence.

p.label: Unsigned birth certificate
p.facts: Gina sues Hugo for support of her son, presenting a birth certificate naming Hugo as the father. Hugo did not sign it or help prepare it.
p.q: Is the birth certificate enough to prove paternity?
alac: No. The birth certificate is not enough.

The law provides that filiation may be proved by the record of birth. Jurisprudence provides that a birth certificate not signed by the alleged father, or prepared without his participation, is not competent evidence of paternity.
Here, Hugo neither signed nor helped prepare the birth certificate.
Therefore, it does not prove his paternity, and other evidence is needed.
p.key: Perla v. Baring: participation of the father is the key.

p.label: Suit after the father died
p.facts: Ivy's alleged father died in 2025. In 2026, Ivy, an illegitimate child, sues his estate, relying only on testimony that he treated her as his daughter for years.
p.q: Will the action prosper?
p.hint: What evidence, and when must she sue?
alac: No. The action is barred.

The law provides that an illegitimate child whose action is based on open and continuous possession of status or other secondary evidence may bring the action only during the lifetime of the alleged parent.
Here, Ivy relies only on secondary evidence, open and continuous possession of status, and she sued after her alleged father's death.
Therefore, her action can no longer prosper.
p.key: TWIST: secondary evidence → sue while the parent is alive. Primary evidence → during the child's lifetime.

P.title: Legitimation
P.rule: A child conceived and born outside marriage is legitimated by the parents' subsequent valid marriage, if at conception they had no impediment to marry each other, or the only impediment was minority.

p.label: Single parents marry
p.facts: Jun and Kaye, both single and 25, had a child in 2023. They married in 2025.
p.q: Is the child legitimated?
alac: Yes. The child is legitimated.

The law provides that children conceived and born outside wedlock of parents who, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other may be legitimated by their subsequent valid marriage, with effect retroacting to the child's birth.
Here, Jun and Kaye were both single and of age, with no impediment, when the child was conceived. They later validly married.
Therefore, the child is legitimated from birth.
p.key: Retroacts to birth.

p.label: Teenage parents
p.facts: Leo was 17 and Mia 16 when their child was conceived. Both were single. They married when both turned 19.
p.q: Is the child legitimated?
alac: Yes. The child is legitimated.

The law provides that children whose parents were disqualified to marry each other at the time of conception only because either or both were below 18 may be legitimated by the parents' subsequent valid marriage.
Here, the only impediment at conception was that Leo and Mia were below 18.
Therefore, their later valid marriage legitimated the child.
p.key: RA 9858 added the minority exception.

p.label: Father was married to someone else
p.facts: Ned, validly married to Ora, had a child with Pam. Ora later died, and Ned married Pam.
p.q: Is the child legitimated?
p.hint: Was there an impediment at conception?
alac: No. The child is not legitimated.
The law provides that only children of parents who, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, other than minority, may be legitimated.
Here, when the child was conceived, Ned was validly married to Ora, which was an impediment to marrying Pam. Ora's later death does not erase the impediment that existed at conception.
Therefore, the child is not legitimated and remains illegitimate.
p.key: TWIST: look at the time of CONCEPTION, not the marriage.

P.title: Who may adopt; joint adoption
P.rule: A Filipino adopter must be at least 25, qualified, and at least 16 years older than the adoptee (waivable for a biological parent or the spouse of the adoptee's parent); spouses must adopt jointly, with three exceptions.

p.label: Married man adopts alone
p.facts: Quin, 35, married to Rita, wants to adopt an orphan with a CDCLAA. Rita does not want to join the application. They are not legally separated.
p.q: May Quin adopt the child alone?
alac: No. Quin cannot adopt alone.

The law provides that spouses shall jointly adopt, except when one spouse adopts the legitimate child of the other, when one spouse adopts his or her own illegitimate child with the other's consent, or when the spouses are legally separated.
Here, the child is an orphan, not Rita's legitimate child or Quin's illegitimate child, and the spouses are not legally separated.
Therefore, Quin and Rita must adopt jointly; Quin cannot adopt alone.
p.key: Know the three exceptions by heart.

p.label: Stepfather adopts stepchild
p.facts: Sam, 28, married Tina, who has a 15-year-old legitimate son from her first marriage. Sam alone applies to adopt the boy.
p.q: May Sam adopt alone, despite the age gap of only 13 years?
p.hint: Two rules: joint adoption and the age gap.
alac: Yes. Sam may adopt the boy alone.
The law provides that a spouse may adopt alone the legitimate child of the other spouse, and that the 16-year age difference is not required when the adopter is the spouse of the adoptee's parent.
Here, the boy is Tina's legitimate child, and Sam is Tina's spouse.
Therefore, both the joint-adoption rule and the age-gap rule are excepted, and Sam may adopt alone.
p.key: Stepparent adoption fits both exceptions.

p.label: Young adopter
p.facts: Uma, 23, single, financially stable and of good moral character, wants to adopt her 2-year-old niece, who has a CDCLAA.
p.q: May Uma adopt?
alac: No. Uma is not yet qualified.
The law provides that a Filipino adopter must generally be at least 25 years old, among other qualifications.
Here, Uma is only 23, even though she meets the other qualifications.
Therefore, she cannot adopt yet.
p.key: TWIST: the minimum age under RA 11642 is 25. Older reviewers may show a different rule.

P.title: Rescission of adoption
P.rule: Only the adoptee may seek rescission, on grounds such as repeated maltreatment, attempt on the adoptee's life, sexual assault or violence, or abandonment; the adopter's remedy is disinheritance.

p.label: Adopter wants out
p.facts: Vera adopted Will in 2015. In 2026, Will, now 20, is rude and refuses to visit her. Vera files a petition to rescind the adoption.
p.q: Will the petition prosper?
alac: No. The petition will not prosper.
The law provides that rescission of adoption may be sought only by the adoptee. Jurisprudence provides that the adopter's remedy is to disinherit the adoptee for causes provided by law.
Here, the petition was filed by Vera, the adopter.
Therefore, the petition will not prosper; Vera may only disinherit Will if a legal ground exists.
p.key: Lahom v. Sibulo.

p.label: Adoptee abused
p.facts: Xian, 16, adopted at age 5, has been repeatedly beaten and insulted by his adoptive father despite counseling.
p.q: May the adoption be rescinded?
alac: Yes. The adoption may be rescinded at Xian's instance.
The law provides that the adoptee, with assistance if a minor, may seek rescission on grounds including repeated physical or verbal maltreatment by the adopter despite counseling.
Here, Xian is the adoptee, and he has been repeatedly beaten and insulted despite counseling.
Therefore, the adoption may be rescinded, and his biological parents' parental authority is restored if he is still a minor.
p.key: Effect: parental authority of the biological parents is restored for a minor.

p.label: Adoptee's grades
p.facts: Yuri's adoptive parents scold him for low grades and take away his phone for a week. Yuri, 15, wants to rescind the adoption.
p.q: Is there a ground to rescind?
alac: No. There is no ground to rescind.

The law provides that rescission is allowed only on serious grounds such as repeated physical or verbal maltreatment despite counseling, an attempt on the adoptee's life, sexual assault or violence, or abandonment.
Here, scolding for low grades and taking away a phone for a week are reasonable discipline, not repeated maltreatment.
Therefore, Yuri has no ground to rescind.
p.key: TWIST: discipline ≠ maltreatment. The grounds are serious.

P.title: Support
P.rule: Support covers sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical care, education (even beyond majority), and transportation; it is owed by the persons listed in Art. 195 in the order of Art. 199, and payable only from demand.

p.label: College student, age 21
p.facts: Zoe, 21, is in her third year of college. Her father stopped giving support when she turned 18. She sends him a demand letter, then sues.
p.q: Is Zoe entitled to support for her education?
alac: Yes. Zoe is entitled to support for her education.

The law provides that support includes education, which covers schooling or training for a profession, trade, or vocation, even beyond the age of majority. Parents and their children are obliged to support each other.
Here, Zoe is the father's child and is completing a college course.
Therefore, she is entitled to support, payable from the date of her demand.
p.key: Education support continues beyond 18.

p.label: Grandparents step in
p.facts: Ara's husband abandoned the family and cannot be found; Ara is unemployed. Her children's paternal grandparents are wealthy. Ara sues the grandparents for support of the children and of herself.
p.q: Are the grandparents liable?
p.hint: Order of liability; who is entitled.
alac: The grandparents are liable for the children's support, but not for Ara's.

The law provides that legitimate ascendants and descendants are obliged to support each other, and that when the parents cannot, the obligation falls on ascendants in the nearest degree. Jurisprudence provides that in-laws are not among those entitled to support.
Here, the parents cannot give support, so the paternal grandparents are liable to support the grandchildren. Ara is their daughter-in-law, who is not among those entitled.
Therefore, the grandparents must support the children but not Ara.
p.key: Lim v. Lim.

p.label: Waiver of future support
p.facts: In 2024, Bea agreed with her ex-partner Cal that, in exchange for P200,000, she would never ask for future support for their son. In 2026, she sues for support.
p.q: Does the agreement bar the suit?
alac: No. The agreement does not bar the suit.
The law provides that the right to support cannot be renounced, and that future support cannot be the subject of a compromise.
Here, the agreement waived the son's future support in exchange for money.
Therefore, the waiver is void, and the son may claim support. The P200,000 may be considered in fixing the amount.
p.key: TWIST: future support can't be waived or compromised; support in ARREARS can.

P.title: Custody and the tender-age rule
P.rule: When parents separate, the court awards custody considering the child's best interest and the choice of a child over 7; no child under 7 shall be separated from the mother absent compelling reasons.

p.label: Mother works abroad on leave
p.facts: Dan and Eva separate. Their daughter is 4. Eva works as a nurse in Manila; Dan is wealthier. Dan asks for custody, saying he can provide more.
p.q: Who should have custody?
alac: Eva should have custody.

The law provides that no child under seven years of age shall be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons to order otherwise. Jurisprudence provides that compelling reasons include neglect, abandonment, unemployment, immorality, drug addiction, or insanity.
Here, the daughter is 4. Eva's job and Dan's greater wealth are not compelling reasons.
Therefore, custody should be with Eva.
p.key: Wealth is not a compelling reason.

p.label: Child of 10 chooses
p.facts: Fred and Gail separate. Their 10-year-old son, after counseling, chooses to live with Fred. Both parents are fit.
p.q: Who should have custody?
alac: Fred should have custody.
The law provides that in awarding custody when parents separate, the court shall consider the choice of a child over seven years of age, unless the parent chosen is unfit.
Here, the son is 10, chose Fred, and Fred is fit.
Therefore, the court should award custody to Fred.
p.key: Over 7: the child's choice weighs heavily, unless the parent is unfit.

p.label: Mother with drug addiction
p.facts: Hana and Ivan separate. Their son is 3. Hana has a proven drug addiction and has left the child alone for days.
p.q: Who should have custody?
alac: Ivan should have custody.
The law provides that a child under seven shall not be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons. Jurisprudence recognizes drug addiction and neglect as compelling reasons.
Here, Hana has a proven drug addiction and has left the child alone for days.
Therefore, there are compelling reasons, and custody should go to Ivan.
p.key: TWIST: the tender-age rule yields to compelling reasons.

P.title: Special parental authority and liability
P.rule: Schools, administrators, teachers, and child-care institutions have special parental authority over minors in their custody, including authorized off-campus activities, and are principally and solidarily liable, with the parents subsidiarily liable; the act must be the proximate cause.

p.label: Injury during class
p.facts: During a supervised PE class, 12-year-old Jake pushed classmate Kim, who broke her arm. The teacher was on her phone and did not watch the students.
p.q: Who is liable for Kim's injury?
alac: The school, its administrators, and the teacher are principally and solidarily liable; Jake's parents are subsidiarily liable.

The law provides that the school, its administrators, and teachers have special parental authority over minors under their supervision, and are principally and solidarily liable for damages caused by the acts of the minors, while the parents are subsidiarily liable; the defense is proper diligence.
Here, Jake, a minor, injured Kim during class while under the teacher's supervision, and the teacher was not watching.
Therefore, the school and teacher are principally liable, and Jake's parents are subsidiarily liable.
p.key: Principal + solidary = school; subsidiary = parents.

p.label: Off-campus field trip
p.facts: During a school-approved field trip to a museum, a 13-year-old student damaged a display while teachers chatted in the lobby.
p.q: Is the school liable even though the incident was off campus?
p.hint: Does special authority extend outside school?
alac: Yes. The school is liable.
The law provides that special parental authority applies to all authorized activities, whether inside or outside the premises of the school.
Here, the field trip was school-approved, and the teachers were not supervising.
Therefore, the school, administrators, and teachers are principally and solidarily liable.
p.key: Authorized off-campus activities are covered.

p.label: Mechanical failure
p.facts: During a school campaign, a student rode a jeep driven by a minor student. The jeep overturned because its steering wheel guide suddenly detached, killing a passenger. The driving was careful.
p.q: Is the school liable?
alac: No. The school is not liable.

The law provides for the school's liability under special parental authority. Jurisprudence provides that this liability requires that the negligence of the school or the act of the minor be the proximate cause of the injury.
Here, the proximate cause was the detachment of the steering wheel guide, a mechanical defect, not the school's negligence or the minor's driving.
Therefore, the school is not liable.
p.key: TWIST: St. Mary's Academy v. Carpitanos. Check proximate cause.

P.title: Funerals
P.rule: The right and duty to make funeral arrangements follows the order for support (spouse, descendants, ascendants, siblings), respecting the deceased's wishes; among equals, the oldest is preferred.

p.label: Wife vs. live-in partner
p.facts: Leon, legally married to Mona, lived with Nina for 15 years before he died. He left no written wishes. Nina buried him in her family's plot without telling Mona.
p.q: Who had the right to decide where to bury Leon?
alac: Mona, the legal wife, had the right.

The law provides that the duty and right to make funeral arrangements follow the order of persons obliged to support, beginning with the spouse. Jurisprudence provides that a common-law partner has no right superior to the legal spouse.
Here, Mona is Leon's legal wife, and Leon left no written wishes. Nina is only a live-in partner.
Therefore, Mona had the right to decide, and she may seek the transfer of the remains.
p.key: Valino v. Adriano.

p.label: Children of the same degree
p.facts: Olga, a widow, died with no expressed wishes. Her two children, Pat (45) and Rey (40), disagree on cremation.
p.q: Whose decision prevails?
alac: Pat's decision prevails.
The law provides that among descendants of the same degree, the oldest shall be preferred in making funeral arrangements.
Here, Pat and Rey are both children, and Pat is older.
Therefore, Pat's decision prevails.
p.key: Oldest among equals; among ascendants, the paternal side.

p.label: Deceased's written wish
p.facts: Sara, a widow, left a signed note asking to be cremated. Her oldest son wants a traditional burial.
p.q: Must her wish be followed?
alac: Yes. Her wish must be followed.
The law provides that the funeral shall be in accordance with the expressed wishes of the deceased; in their absence, his religious beliefs or affiliation shall determine the funeral rites.
Here, Sara expressed in a signed note her wish to be cremated.
Therefore, her son must follow her wish, even though he would otherwise have the right to decide.
p.key: TWIST: the deceased's own wishes come before the order of relatives.

P.title: Absence and presumptive death
P.rule: A person may be declared absent after 2 years without news (5 if he left an administrator); presumed dead after 7 years (10 for succession, 5 if over 75) or 4 years in danger cases; remarriage needs 4 years (2 in danger cases), a well-founded belief, and a judicial declaration.

p.label: Declaration of absence
p.facts: Tito left home in 2023 without news and without leaving anyone to manage his properties. In 2026, his wife asks the court to declare him absent.
p.q: May Tito be declared absent?
alac: Yes. Tito may be declared absent.

The law provides that two years having elapsed without any news about the absentee or since the receipt of the last news, an absence may be declared, or five years if he left a person in charge of his property.
Here, Tito has been gone without news for about three years and left no administrator.
Therefore, he may be declared absent, the declaration taking effect six months after publication.
p.key: 2 years (no administrator) vs. 5 years (with administrator).

p.label: Seafarer lost at sea
p.facts: Ugo's ship sank in 2023 and he was never found. In 2025, his wife Vina wants to remarry.
p.q: May Vina remarry, and what must she do?
alac: Yes, after obtaining a judicial declaration of presumptive death.

The law provides that for purposes of remarriage, the absent spouse must have been absent for four consecutive years, or two years where there is danger of death, and the present spouse must have a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is dead and obtain a declaration of presumptive death in a summary proceeding.
Here, Ugo was on a ship that sank, a danger-of-death case, and has been missing for two years.
Therefore, Vina may remarry after obtaining a judicial declaration of presumptive death.
p.key: Remarriage always needs a COURT declaration.

p.label: Half-hearted search
p.facts: Wena's husband left after a quarrel in 2021. She asked two relatives about him and posted once on social media. In 2025 she petitions for a declaration of presumptive death to remarry.
p.q: Will the petition be granted?
alac: No. The petition will not be granted.

The law provides that the present spouse must have a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is dead. Jurisprudence requires diligent and reasonable efforts to find the absent spouse, strictly applied.
Here, Wena only asked two relatives and posted once online. These are passive efforts that do not show a diligent search.
Therefore, she has no well-founded belief, and the petition will be denied.
p.key: TWIST: 4 years is not enough by itself (Republic v. Cantor).

P.title: Correcting civil register entries
P.rule: Clerical errors, first name, day and month of birth, and clerical errors in sex may be corrected administratively; substantial changes such as citizenship, legitimacy, or civil status need an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding.

p.label: Wrong birth month
p.facts: Xena's birth certificate shows her birth month as “June” instead of “July.” All her school and baptismal records show July.
p.q: How may she correct it?
alac: She may file a petition with the local civil registrar for administrative correction.
The law provides that the city or municipal civil registrar may correct clerical or typographical errors and change the day and month of birth in the civil register without a court order.
Here, the error concerns only the month of birth and is shown by consistent records.
Therefore, Xena may correct it administratively.
p.key: Day and month = administrative; YEAR = judicial.

p.label: Ridiculous first name
p.facts: Yogi's first name in his birth certificate is “Bobo.” He has always used “Robert” in school and work.
p.q: How may he change his first name?
alac: He may petition the local civil registrar for a change of first name.

The law provides that a first name may be changed administratively when it is ridiculous or extremely difficult to write or pronounce, or when the new first name has been habitually and continuously used and publicly known.
Here, “Bobo” is ridiculous, and he has habitually used “Robert.”
Therefore, he may change his first name administratively.
p.key: Know the three grounds for a change of first name.

p.label: Change of legitimacy status
p.facts: Zack's birth certificate states that he is legitimate, but his parents never married. He wants it corrected to illegitimate.
p.q: May the civil registrar correct it administratively?
alac: No. It requires a judicial proceeding under Rule 108.

The law provides that only clerical or typographical errors and the specific items allowed by law may be corrected administratively. Jurisprudence provides that substantial changes, such as those affecting legitimacy or civil status, require an adversarial proceeding under Rule 108.
Here, the change affects Zack's legitimacy, a substantial matter.
Therefore, he must file a petition in court under Rule 108.
p.key: TWIST: status changes are never “clerical.”

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: A family home retains its status for as long as the husband, wife, and children, if any, live in the premises.
The Family Code provisions on family homes apply to all existing family residences, deemed constituted when occupied before the Code took effect.
A family home remains as such, even with the death of the constitutor, for 10 years or as long as there is a minor beneficiary, unless the court finds compelling reasons.
A house and lot under a conditional sale on installments, where the seller reserves ownership to guarantee payment, cannot become a family home.
Under the Civil Code, a family home can be constituted only judicially, by petition for court approval.
XP.x: Choice C restates Art. 159 correctly. Choice D contradicts Art. 156, which allows a property under such a conditional sale to be a family home. Choice E is also wrong: the Civil Code allowed both judicial and extrajudicial constitution. If “does not belong” means the false statement, the answer is D (or E).

XP.q: Which of the following is NOT a ground for the modification of a marriage settlement?
o: A spouse leaves the conjugal home without just cause
One spouse publicly engages in extramarital affairs
A couple files a joint manifestation of reconciliation after a decree of legal separation
One spouse is convicted of a crime carrying civil interdiction
XP.x: All may lead to a judicially approved change in the regime: abandonment and civil interdiction are grounds for judicial separation (Art. 135); infidelity can lead to legal separation, which dissolves the regime; reconciliation allows revival (Arts. 66–67).

XP.q: Which of the following is NOT a ground for judicial separation of property?
o: The wife appointed her father as administrator, then left and has not been heard of in the last 4 years
The wife was judicially found grossly negligent toward her illegitimate child and lost parental authority
The husband leaves the family domicile to pursue another woman
The husband willfully neglects or grossly mismanages the common property
The spouse disappears for 4 years without news
XP.x: The key treats A as not a ground because she provided for the administration. But a spouse separated in fact for at least 1 year with reconciliation highly improbable is a ground (Art. 135(6)), and a spouse declared absent is another. Know the key's answer, and be ready to explain both sides if it is an essay.

XP.q: In relation to a family home, which of the following does NOT belong?
XP.x: Art. 158 lists sale, alienation, donation, assignment, and encumbrance as needing written consent. Lease is not in the list, so strictly, lease does not belong.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong in the ACP?
o: All property owned at the time of and acquired during the marriage
Property bought, bartered, or exchanged with exclusive property
Fruits and income of separate property
XP.x: Jewelry, property owned or acquired, and winnings are community property (Arts. 91, 92(2), 95). Under the preferred view, property bought with exclusive money is community. But Art. 92 excludes the fruits and income of gratuitously acquired property and of pre-marriage property of a spouse with legitimate descendants, so E is the likely exception.

XP.q: Which of the following is TRUE?
o: The marriage settlement must be registered at the place of the marriage and where the couple fixes their domicile
An oral prenuptial agreement is void
The future spouses can stipulate when the property regime shall take effect
If the marriage does not take place, stipulations not dependent on the marriage remain valid
Only the future spouses are parties to the settlement, and both must be single and at least 18
XP.x: Art. 81. Registration is in the local civil registry where the marriage contract is recorded and the proper property registries, not the domicile. The regime starts at the celebration; a contrary stipulation is void (Art. 88). Whether an oral settlement is void or unenforceable is debated, so B is not clearly true.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: The husband borrows money for the family business
Renovation expenses by the woman before the marriage for the house that became the family home
The wife gives P20,000 so her daughter can enroll in a speech class
The wife borrows money to buy a car for her exclusive use, with the husband's written consent
XP.x: Donations to common children for self-improvement are chargeable only if made by BOTH spouses (Art. 94(8)). The others are chargeable: loans for the family business, ante-nuptial debts that benefited the family, and debts contracted with the other's consent.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: Brothers and sisters, whether full or half-blood
XP.x: The likely basis is the codal wording of Art. 150 (family relations), which says “parents and children” without the word illegitimate. But note that illegitimate children ARE covered by support under Art. 195(4). Follow the key in an MCQ, but know the support rule.

XP.q: Which of the following is FALSE?
o: If the parties expressly stipulate that their regime is neither ACP nor CPG but do not say which regime applies, the regime shall not be CSP
For marriages after the Family Code, ACP applies when the parties have no prenuptial agreement and when they stipulate it in a marriage settlement
A prenuptial agreement that subjects only 70% of the couple's properties to ACP is void
When a spouse dies and the survivor remarries before the estate is settled, the regime of the new marriage is CSP
XP.x: B is true: ACP applies by default or by agreement (Art. 75). D is true (Art. 103). C is false: spouses may agree on “any other regime,” including a partial or mixed one; property not agreed as separate is community (Art. 144). Be careful if this appears again.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: How much a child will need until the age of majority
Whether a person is married or not
Whether there are grounds for legal separation
Whether the MTC or the RTC has jurisdiction
XP.x: All cannot be compromised (Art. 2035 CC): future support, civil status, grounds for legal separation, jurisdiction of courts.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: Brothers and sisters and brothers- or sisters-in-law
Widowed spouse as to the property of the deceased spouse
Ascendants, descendants, and relatives by affinity in the same line
XP.x: Under Art. 332 RPC, siblings and in-laws are exempt only if living together; the others are exempt without that condition.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: Open and continuous possession of the status
Admission of filiation in a private handwritten instrument signed by the parent
Evidence allowed by the Rules of Court
XP.x: C is primary evidence (Art. 172, par. 1). The rest are secondary evidence (par. 2).

XP.q: Which of the following is FALSE, of donations propter nuptias?
o: The grounds for revocation are those found in the Civil Code
The only limitation is that it must not impair future legitimes
XP.x: DPN may include future property, governed by the rules on wills (Art. 84), so D is false. E is also false: there is the 1/5 limit when the regime is not ACP. The grounds are mainly in Art. 86 of the Family Code, so C is questionable too.

XP.q: Which of the following is FALSE, in relation to CPG liquidation?
o: The conjugal dwelling and lot go to the spouse with whom the majority of the common children choose to remain
Delivery of exclusive property follows only after the debts and obligations of the CPG are paid
The CPG must reimburse a spouse if it used exclusive property
The first step is to make an inventory listing all the conjugal property
XP.x: The inventory must list the conjugal property AND the exclusive property of each spouse, separately (Art. 129(1)). The trap is the word “all the conjugal property” only.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
o: Minor repairs of the family home
Emergency loan by the wife alone, without the husband's consent, for a child's hospitalization
Real property taxes on the wife's exclusive property used by both spouses
Transportation expenses of the children from the first marriage
Bar review expenses contracted before the marriage by the husband
XP.x: All are chargeable: repairs, debts that benefited the family, taxes on separate property used by the family, support of legitimate children of either spouse, and self-improvement expenses.

XP.q: Which of the following is FALSE (administration of property)?
o: In a disagreement on an act of administration, the wife may go to court to declare the husband's act void
A sale by one spouse without the other's consent is unenforceable
The period to challenge a sale made without consent is 10 years
Alterations of conjugal property need the consent of both spouses
XP.best: B, C, and D are false
XP.x: Under Arts. 96/124: the husband's decision prevails and the wife may seek a proper remedy within 5 years (not “declare void”, not 10 years); a sale without consent is VOID, not unenforceable. The key's answer is unclear; know the codal rules.

XP.q: Which of the following does NOT belong?
XP.x: The rest dissolve an existing ACP or CPG. A void marriage never had an ACP or CPG (Art. 147 or 148 governs), except an Art. 40 subsequent marriage.

XP.q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: A DPN of more than 1/5 of the donor's property is void
A DPN made during the celebration of the marriage is considered an ordinary donation
In a CPG or CSP regime, there is no limit on how much the spouses can donate to each other after the marriage
The 1/5 limit applies to DPN between future spouses who agree on a regime other than ACP
XP.x: Donations between spouses during the marriage are void, except moderate gifts on family rejoicing (Art. 87), whatever the regime.

XP.q: True or False: A stipulation in a CPG that excludes a spouse from any share in the losses is void.
XP.x: Partnership rules apply suppletorily; a stipulation excluding a partner from losses is void.

XP.q: True or False: A widower with 2 illegitimate children marries again. All his property, and its fruits and income, are his exclusive property.
XP.x: Art. 92(3) excludes only when the spouse has LEGITIMATE descendants by a former marriage.

XP.q: True or False: A loan made by the wife alone for the family business is presumed to redound to the benefit of the family.
XP.x: A loan for the spouse's own business or profession is presumed to benefit the family (Ayala Investment).

XP.q: True or False: Under ACP, a car bought for the exclusive use of the wife is her exclusive property.
XP.x: Property for personal and exclusive use is excluded, except jewelry (Art. 92(2)).

XP.q: Properties are owned by the couple according to their respective contributions.
XP.x: Actual contribution, in proportion.

XP.q: This is also called special co-ownership.
This is also called limited co-ownership.
Salaries and wages are owned by both in equal shares.
Properties are presumed obtained through joint efforts.
When conjugal property is not enough, liability falls on separate property, and the spouses are solidarily liable.
XP.x: Arts. 121 and 94 both make the spouses solidarily liable.

XP.q: Liability to creditors is solidary, but internally proportionate to the spouses' income.
Expenses for the preservation of separate property are charged even if the property is not used by the family.
XP.x: Art. 121(5); ACP requires use by the family (Art. 94(5)).

XP.q: There is co-ownership between the spouses.
Only the net profits are divided upon dissolution.
Personal obligations during the marriage that benefit only one spouse are charged to that spouse's separate property.
The donee spouse knowingly contracts a subsequent void marriage.
The spouses were married by a solemnizing officer who had no authority.
XP.x: Void marriage → Art. 86(1).

XP.q: Donation made in the marriage settlement, but the marriage was not celebrated.
XP.x: Art. 81.

XP.q: The donee is less than 18 years old.
XP.x: Void marriage (Art. 35(1)) → Art. 86(1).

XP.q: The donee spouse suffers because of the husband's (donor's) serious drug addiction.
XP.x: The donee is the innocent spouse; no ground to revoke.

XP.q: The donee imputes to the donor the crime of attempted homicide against the donee's children.
XP.x: Imputing a crime is not ingratitude when the crime was committed against the donee's own children (Art. 765(2)).

XP.q: The spouses, both 20, married without parental consent.
The donee remarries after a declaration of presumptive death obtained in bad faith.
The donee remarries after a judicial declaration of presumptive death (no bad faith stated).
XP.x: A subsequent marriage under Art. 41 is valid, and donations remain valid if there is no bad faith (Art. 43(3)). No Art. 86 ground appears.

XP.q: The donee spouse did not know that the other spouse had an STD at the time of the marriage.
XP.x: The donee is the innocent party. Art. 86(3) allows revocation only if the DONEE acted in bad faith.

XP.q: Marriage between third cousins.
XP.x: Not a prohibited marriage; it is valid.

XP.q: The donee is guilty of adultery.
XP.x: Upon legal separation, the innocent spouse MAY revoke donations to the guilty spouse within 5 years (Arts. 64, 86(4)). It is not automatic.

XP.q: In a void subsequent marriage where both parties connived (both in bad faith); the donor is the man and the donee is the woman.
XP.x: Art. 44 says all donations by reason of marriage are revoked by operation of law.

XP.q: The donee spouse was imprisoned for 2 years.
XP.x: Imprisonment is a ground for legal separation only if MORE than 6 years. Two years is not a ground under Art. 86.

XP.q: A donation propter nuptias where the marriage was called off.
XP.best: Void if in the marriage settlement; otherwise revocable
XP.x: Art. 81 for settlements; Art. 86(1) otherwise.

XP.q: The donee spouse contracts a subsequent void marriage, but in good faith.
XP.x: Void marriage → Art. 86(1); good faith only prevents automatic revocation.

XP.q: The spouses married with an expired marriage license.
XP.x: No valid license → void → Art. 86(1).

XP.q: The donee commits an offense against the donor's spouse.
XP.x: Ingratitude (Art. 765(1)).

XP.q: The donee spouse has a serious and incurable STD.
XP.x: Voidable marriage; revocable if annulled and the donee acted in bad faith (Art. 86(3)).

XP.q: The donee was forced, under pain of death, to marry the offending spouse.
XP.x: The donee is the victim, not in bad faith. Art. 86(3) requires the DONEE's bad faith.
